Female Marbled newts attain a larger ultimate snout-vent length than males, reaching up to 7.55 centimeters [Li = up to 7.55 centimeters] in total body size, a dimorphism that is common among European newts and is thought to confer advantages in fecundity. Males, by contrast, typically do not exceed 6.85 centimeters [Li = 6.85 centimeters] in snout-vent length. This sexual size difference is reflected in body mass as well, with adult females achieving an ultimate wet weight of approximately 10.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 10.6 grams], a value estimated from the closely related and morphologically similar Triturus cristatus. Adult males, based on the same comparative reference, reach a lower asymptotic mass of about 9.4 grams [Wwi = about 9.4 grams]. These disparities in both length and mass likely arise from differential selective pressures, where larger female body size is linked to greater clutch volume, while male reproductive success may depend more on competitive behaviors than on sheer body dimensions.

Development begins within a fertilised ovum encased in a protective jelly coat, and the timing of hatching is strongly temperature-dependent. When eggs are incubated at a constant 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C], the period from oviposition to eclosion lasts approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days], though field records indicate a broader range of 14 to 21 days depending on microhabitat thermal regimes. The newly emerged aquatic larva, or endotrophic tadpole, is remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This minute mass is a direct consequence of the modest egg diameter, which measures roughly 2 millimeters. The yolk-laden egg thus provides just enough endogenous nutrition to sustain the larva through the earliest developmental stages until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins on small aquatic invertebrates and algae.

Following hatching, the free-swimming larva embarks on a prolonged period of aquatic growth. At a water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis averages approximately 84 days , corresponding to about 2.5 to 3 months of larval development. This post-larval transformation involves dramatic body plan reorganisation, including the resorption of gills and the development of limbs, culminating in the emergence of a terrestrial juvenile. During the larval phase, the tadpoles are actively growing and filter-feeding, accumulating the energy reserves necessary to support the metamorphic climax. The thermal regime of 9 °C represents a relatively cool breeding pond environment, and in warmer waters, this developmental period can be considerably shortened, demonstrating the species' phenotypic plasticity in response to local conditions.

Sexual maturation in Marbled newts is also heavily influenced by environmental temperature and exhibits a clear sexual bimaturism. Under conditions where the mean annual temperature averages 9 °C [T = 9 °C], females attain puberty at approximately 6 years since birth [tp = approximately 6 years since birth], a relatively protracted period for a urodele amphibian of this size. Males, in contrast, reach sexual maturity sooner, at about 5 years since birth [tp = about 5 years since birth], reflecting a common pattern among vertebrates where earlier male maturation is selected for by the operational sex at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C] ratio. The onset of gonadal maturation in both sexes marks the transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively active adult capable of participating in seasonal breeding aggregations, which typically occur in early spring when individuals migrate to ancestral ponds.

The maximum reproductive rate of the Marbled newt is constrained by its single annual clutch. At a reference temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females produce between 200 and 380 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 200 and 380 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. This annual reproductive output, combined with a maximum lifespan of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] under similar thermal conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparity over high immediate fecundity. The female asymptotic body mass of 10.6 grams [Wwi = 10.6 grams] therefore supports a large clutch relative to body size, while the long lifespan, recorded as 9125 days [am = 9125 days] in some captive studies, allows for many years of repeated breeding effort at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This slow-paced, investment-oriented life history is typical of long-lived salamandrids inhabiting stable, predictable aquatic environments.
